# Block 5: Instructions and skills {.unnumbered} The previous block showed that the further up the autonomy ladder an assistant works, the more its unstated assumptions land in your files. This block is how you state your conventions once, so you do not repeat them in every prompt. There are two mechanisms, distinguished by when they load: - **Instructions** live in an instruction fileA file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project’s standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees. that loads into every conversation automatically. Use it for what is always true of the project: structure, style, reproducibility rules. - **Skills** load only when invoked by name or judged relevant from their description. A skillA folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description. suits a procedure you need sometimes: producing a publication figure, cleaning data against a codebook, reviewing code. Both are requests. The model usually follows them, but nothing guarantees it. Rules that must hold every time belong in the enforced controls of [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd). *⏱ ~45 minutes* ## Part A: Instructions ### Where Claude Code looks | File | Claude Code | Posit Assistant | |---|---|---| | `AGENTS.md` (repository root) | Via an import in `CLAUDE.md` | Read as project memory | | `CLAUDE.md` | Read at the start of every conversation | — | This course uses **one source of truth**: conventions live in `AGENTS.md`, and `CLAUDE.md` contains a single line that imports it: ```text @AGENTS.md ``` Other tools read `AGENTS.md` too (see *Going further*), so one file serves them all. Skills, in Part B, follow the same idea: one master copy, read by each tool from where it looks. :::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="Which files each tool reads: CLAUDE.md imports AGENTS.md; skills are copied from .agents/skills to .claude/skills"} ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Instruction files: loaded into every conversation ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `CLAUDE.md`, one line: `@AGENTS.md` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} imports ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `AGENTS.md`: your conventions ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} read by ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Claude Code, through `CLAUDE.md` ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Skills: loaded when invoked or judged relevant ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `.agents/skills/house-figures/` (the master copy) ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} you copy ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `.claude/skills/house-figures/` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} read by ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Claude Code ::: ::::: ::: {.dia-caption} Posit Assistant reads `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/` directly, so it needs neither `CLAUDE.md` nor the copy. ::: :::::: ### Writing instructions that work - **One instruction per line.** Short, concrete statements are easier to check than paragraphs, for the model and for you. - **Describe what you actually do.** An instruction your existing code breaks sends the model mixed signals. The test is whether your own scripts obey it. - **Be specific.** "Use the native pipe `|>`" can be checked; "write clean, idiomatic code" cannot. - **Keep it short.** The file loads into every request. Anthropic advises keeping Claude Code's always-loaded file under about 200 lines; aim far lower. - **Add a rule when a mistake repeats.** If the assistant gets the same convention wrong twice, that convention belongs in the file. A one-off correction in chat is forgotten in the next conversation. - **Do not put guarantees here.** "Never edit raw data" is worth stating, but enforce it with the controls in [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd). ### Activity: Build and test your AGENTS.md You start from a provided draft rather than a blank page. Your job is to make it describe *your* practice, then prove that Claude Code reads it. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Adapt, connect, verify (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} Work in your workshop repository, committed and clean. **1. Baseline.** With no `AGENTS.md` present, start Claude Code in `plan` mode. **In the terminal:** ```bash claude --permission-mode plan ``` **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot of mass_post_g by treatment arm. ``` Keep the answer. **2. Copy the starting draft.** Create `AGENTS.md` in the repository root containing the draft below. It includes a canaryA fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.: a fixed first line the assistant is asked to put in any R code it writes, so you can see whether the file was loaded. ```markdown # Project conventions: voles analysis ## Canary When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block: # agents-md: active v1 ## Structure - Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified. - Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/. - Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/. ## R style - Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment. - Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F. - Build every path with here::here(). Never use setwd() or rm(list = ls()). - Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types. ## Reproducibility - Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before adding a package. - Set a seed immediately before any random step. - Every script must run in a fresh R session. ## Data integrity - Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment. - Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic. ## Statistics - Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory. - Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code. ## Working with me - Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval. - Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/. ``` **3. Make it yours.** Delete any rule you do not actually follow. Then add one style convention you genuinely follow that the draft does not state, and one reproducibility or statistical convention you always apply. Keep the canary line. Later blocks rely on the "Statistics" and "Working with me" rules, so keep those too. **4. Connect Claude Code.** Create `CLAUDE.md` in the repository root containing only the line `@AGENTS.md`. **5. Verify.** Commit. Then leave Claude Code (`/exit`) and start it again from the repository root, so it loads the new files at the start of the conversation, and repeat the step 1 prompt. - If the canary appears, the file is being loaded. - If the canary is missing, the file is not reaching Claude Code. Check the file location, the `@AGENTS.md` line in `CLAUDE.md`, and that you started Claude Code from the repository root. - A canary shows that the file was **loaded**, not that every rule was **followed**. Check the plot code against each rule you wrote. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Posit Assistant reads `AGENTS.md` directly as project memory, so it needs no `CLAUDE.md`. Instead of copying the draft, you can have a short conversation about your conventions and run `/savememory`. If the canary is missing, check that you trusted the workspace. ::: :::: ::: ## Part B: Skills A skill is a folder containing a `SKILL.md` file, and optionally scripts, templates and reference files. Its front matterThe block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill’s name and description, or a Quarto document’s options., the block between two lines of three dashes at the top of `SKILL.md`, carries a `name` and a `description`. Skills follow the open Agent Skills specification, so one skill can serve several tools. Two parts decide whether a skill works: - **The description is the trigger.** The assistant reads descriptions to decide which skill is relevant. "Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report, poster or paper" loads when it should; "for plots" loads erratically. Invoking a skill by name (`/skill-name`) does not depend on the description. - **The body is a procedure:** when to use the skill, the steps, hard rules, and a final check. Because a skill loads only when used, it can be longer than an instruction file. For a skill that writes files or has other side effects, set `disable-model-invocation: true` in the front matter, so it runs only when you invoke it by name. Claude Code and Posit Assistant both support this field. ### Where skills live | Location in the repository | Claude Code | Posit Assistant | |---|---|---| | `.agents/skills//` | — | Yes | | `.claude/skills//` | Yes | — | | `.posit/assistant/skills//` | — | Yes | This course keeps the master copy of each skill in `.agents/skills/`, which other tools also read, and **copies** the folder into `.claude/skills/` for Claude Code. If you change a skill, copy it again. On macOS or Linux you can use a symbolic linkA file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler. instead, so there is only one copy: **In the terminal (macOS or Linux):** ```bash mkdir -p .claude/skills ln -s ../../.agents/skills/house-figures .claude/skills/house-figures ``` On Windows, symbolic links in git need extra configuration, so copy the folder. ### Activity: Write a skill and test it :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} A house figure style (20 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Baseline, before the skill exists.** In Claude Code, ask: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a lab report. ``` Keep the code it gives you. Doing this first, before you create the skill, guarantees the baseline was written without it. **2. Create the skill.** Create `.agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md` containing: ```markdown --- name: house-figures description: >- Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots. --- # House figure style ## Rules 1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar with error bars ("dynamite plot"). 2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same variable to point shape so the figure works without colour. 3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)". 4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12). 5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure. 6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a fitted model and asks for them. ## Before returning code List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why. ``` Then copy the `house-figures` folder into `.claude/skills/`, in your file manager or in the terminal: **In the terminal (macOS, Linux or Git Bash):** ```bash mkdir -p .claude/skills cp -r .agents/skills/house-figures .claude/skills/ ``` **3. With the skill.** Leave Claude Code (`/exit`) and start it again, so it finds the new skill. Invoke the skill by name and ask the same thing: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a lab report. ``` **4. Grade it.** For each of the six rules, record whether the output complies: | Rule | Without skill | With skill | |---|---|---| | 1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot | | | | 2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape | | | | 3. Units in axis titles | | | | 4. `theme_classic(base_size = 12)` | | | | 5. n per group shown | | | | 6. No unrequested p-values | | | Run the code and look at the figure. Code that names the right functions can still produce the wrong picture. **Payoff.** What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and would you use it again for the next figure? **5. Test the trigger.** In a new Claude Code conversation (`/clear`), without naming the skill, ask "Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm" (exploratory, so the skill should *not* load). Then, in another new conversation, ask "Polish this figure for the poster" (it *should* load). If either goes the wrong way, rewrite the description and test again. **6. Test a rule under pressure.** Ask the assistant to "add significance stars between the groups". Rule 6 says it should decline without a fitted model. Note whether it did. A skill is an instruction, not a guarantee. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Posit Assistant reads `.agents/skills/` directly, so you do not need the copy in `.claude/skills/`. Invoke the skill by name in the same way. ::: :::: ::: ### Skills you did not write Each tool ships built-in skills. Claude Code bundles skills such as `/code-review` and `/debug`. Collections of shared skills are published online, for example Anthropic's `anthropics/skills` repository. Before installing a skill someone else wrote, read it. A skill can include scripts that the assistant may run on your machine, and its instructions shape what the assistant does with your files and data. Treat it as you would any code from the internet. *Going further* below gives you one to practise on: `pub-figures`, the ggplot chapter's conventions packaged as a skill. :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **Check:** the canary shows a file was loaded, not that its rules were followed; grade the output rule by rule, and run the figure code. - **Reproduce:** your `AGENTS.md` now states the reproducibility rules (renv, fresh R session, seeds). They are requests; Blocks 7 and 9 check whether the agent kept to them. - **Record:** add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` naming the skill you tested and what you changed in its output. ::: ## Check your understanding **Your canary line does not appear in Claude Code's answers. What is the most likely explanation?**
**What is the essential difference between an instruction file and a skill?**
**A skill fires for quick exploratory plots when you meant it only for publication figures. What should you change first?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ### Instruction and skill files in other tools | File or folder | Posit Assistant | GitHub Copilot | |---|---|---| | `AGENTS.md` (repository root) | Read as project memory | Read by the cloud agent, agent mode and the CLI | | `CLAUDE.md` | — | Read by the cloud agent | | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | Offered for conversion by `/import-instructions` | Read by Copilot | | Path-scoped rules | No equivalent found | `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` with `applyTo` | | `.agents/skills//` | Yes | Yes | | `.claude/skills//` | — | Yes | | `.github/skills//` | — | Yes | Copilot's cloud agent reads both `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, so it may see the conventions twice. That is harmless but wasteful, so keep `CLAUDE.md` to the one import line. Copilot reads both `.agents/skills/` and `.claude/skills/`; if it lists a skill twice, remove one route for Copilot. Posit Assistant also includes built-in skills such as `quarto-authoring` and `r-package-development`. ### A rule for Quarto files only Some rules are right for one kind of file and wrong elsewhere. A chunk option such as `#| echo: false` is meaningful in a `.qmd` file and meaningless in an `.R` script. The test for a scoped rule: would it be *wrong*, not merely irrelevant, in the files it excludes? If not, put it in `AGENTS.md`. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Create and test a scoped rule :::: ::::{.task-container} The rules themselves: ```markdown # Quarto document conventions - Set chunk options with the hashpipe (#|) inside the chunk, not in the {r} header. - Give every chunk a label; prefix figure chunks with fig-. - Every figure chunk sets #| fig-cap:, #| fig-width: and #| fig-height:. - Refer to figures in the text with @fig-..., never by a typed number. - Default to #| echo: false unless the document is a code walkthrough. - Resolve paths with here::here(); never assume the working directory is the document's folder. ``` (The "hashpipe" is the `#|` at the start of a chunk-option line.) Place them where your tool looks: - **Claude Code:** `.claude/rules/quarto.md`, beginning with front matter that restricts it to Quarto files: ```text --- paths: - "**/*.qmd" --- ``` - **Copilot:** `.github/instructions/quarto.instructions.md`, beginning with this front matter: ```text --- applyTo: "**/*.qmd" --- ``` - **Posit Assistant:** no path-scoped instruction file is documented. Add the rules to `AGENTS.md` under a heading such as "When editing .qmd files", or rely on its built-in `quarto-authoring` skill. **Test.** Open a `.qmd` file and ask for a chunk that plots `mass_post_g` by `treatment_arm`. A correct answer uses hashpipe options, a `fig-` label, a caption and `here::here()`. Then ask for the same plot in an `.R` script; the Quarto rules should not appear. If they do not appear in the `.qmd` either, the rule is not loading on your surface. Report what you found; behaviour differs between tools. :::: ::: Every scoped rule is a second copy of a convention to keep in step, once per tool. Use scoped rules sparingly. ### Install a skill bundle and compare `house-figures` is six rules you wrote and can read at a glance. `pub-figures` is the opposite case: the conventions from the ggplot chapter (the chart-type and audience tables, `theme_project()`, colorspace palettes, the colour-vision-deficiency check, the four-element legend, saving in two formats) packaged as a skill of about 200 lines, with R scripts that the assistant sources and adapts. It is a skill you did not write, so you read it before you install it. The bundle contains: ```text pub-figures/ ├── SKILL.md when to use it, the rules, a pre-flight checklist ├── theme-project.R theme_project() and palette functions ├── raincloud-template.R figure skeleton, including saving ├── emmeans-bridge.R model-based significance brackets └── patchwork-template.R multi-panel figure with one shared legend ``` `theme_project()` in this bundle is the full version of the simple `theme_project()` you wrote in the ggplot chapter: the same name and `base_size` argument, with a font, colours for titles and gridlines, and an `axis_type` argument added. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} A skill bundle you did not write :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Read before you install.** Open `SKILL.md` and `theme-project.R` (both are also reproduced below). Find two places where `pub-figures` contradicts your `house-figures` rules. (There are at least two: the palette and the theme.) Find the line that tells the assistant what to do when information is missing. **2. Remove the overlap.** Both skills describe themselves as being for figures in reports, posters and papers, so with both installed you cannot tell which one loaded. Move `house-figures` out of both skills folders (or rename `SKILL.md` inside it) before going on. Overlapping descriptions are a real hazard once you collect skills from several sources. **3. Install.** Unzip the download into `.agents/skills/`, and copy it into `.claude/skills/` for Claude Code, as above. The skill uses ggdist, colorspace, ragg, colorBlindness, emmeans and ggpubr; if your project uses renv and they are not in its lockfile, add them yourself before the test, rather than letting the assistant install packages. **4. Same prompt, new skill.** Restart Claude Code so it finds the skill, then, without naming the skill, ask the prompt from the house-figures activity: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a lab report. ``` Did the skill load from its description alone? Did the assistant ask about the audience, or record a default? **5. Grade it against its own checklist.** The skill ends with a pre-flight checklist. Check the script against each item yourself, rather than accepting the assistant's report that it did. Then run the script: are both a PDF and a PNG in `outputs/figures/`? Run the `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` line it left for you, and look at the result. **6. Test a rule under pressure.** Ask it to "add significance stars between the groups" without fitting a model. The skill says it must insert a legend placeholder rather than invent p-values. Then fit `lm(mass_post_g ~ treatment_arm, data = voles)` and ask again: it should now use the `emmeans-bridge.R` pattern with an adjusted p-value. **7. Compare.** Which skill would you hand to a colleague? Which would you trust without rereading it after an update? A long skill encodes more of your standards, and hides more of them from view. :::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/SKILL.md` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```` markdown --- name: pub-figures description: >- Use when producing a ggplot2 figure intended for sharing outside the immediate session, including manuscript figures, lab reports, posters, talk slides, and public engagement graphics. Do not invoke for diagnostic, exploratory, model-checking, or one-off plots. --- # Publication figures This skill governs production of figures that will be seen by an external audience. It is self-contained: the house rules below apply even if the project has no instruction file. ## House rules - Tidyverse style, native pipe `|>`, `here::here()` for every path. - British spelling in titles, labels, legends and comments. - Never produce pie charts, dual y-axes, 3D effects, or bar charts with error bars ("dynamite plots") when the raw data exist. ## Missing information If information you need is missing (the audience, a variable's unit, the fitted model), ask the user once, in a single message, before writing code. If the user tells you to proceed without it, or you are working unattended (for example as a cloud agent on a pull request), choose the safe default this skill gives, record the choice in a code comment and, if there is one, in the pull request description, and continue. ## Project toolkit The packages this skill assumes are pinned in `renv.lock`: - `ggplot2`, `patchwork`, `here`, `scales` for core plotting, composition, paths, and label formatting. - `ggdist` for raincloud and half-eye distributions: `stat_halfeye()`, `stat_pointinterval()`. - `ggbeeswarm` for moderate-n group displays: `geom_quasirandom()`. - `colorspace` for palettes: `scale_*_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2")`, `scale_*_continuous_sequential(palette = "Viridis")`, `scale_*_continuous_diverging(palette = "Blue-Red")`, and the HCL generators (`sequential_hcl()`, `diverging_hcl()`) used by the brand-seeded scales in `theme-project.R`. - `emmeans` for estimated marginal means and pairwise contrasts: `emmeans(model, specs = "var")`, `pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")`. - `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()` as the rendering layer for emmeans-derived contrasts. Never `ggpubr::stat_compare_means()`, which performs unadjusted pairwise t-tests by default. - `ggh4x` for nested or hierarchical faceting: `facet_nested()`, `facet_nested_wrap()`, `guide_axis_nested()`. - `ragg` for raster output via `ggsave(device = ragg::agg_png)`. - `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` for the colour-vision-deficiency check. - `showtext` (optional) for the project font; without it `theme_project()` falls back to the device's default font. Do not introduce additional plotting packages without amending this list. Do not reach for `cowplot` themes when `theme_minimal()` or `theme_project()` will do. Do not hand-write manual hex colour vectors as data scales: use the `colorspace` palettes or the brand-seeded constructors in `theme-project.R`, both of which keep palettes CVD-checkable. A single fixed colour for a single-group or highlight geom is permitted and is not a "data scale". ## Using the files in this skill Source the theme and palette functions from the skill folder: ```r source(here::here(".agents", "skills", "pub-figures", "theme-project.R")) ``` If the folder was copied into `.claude/skills/` rather than linked, use that path instead. `theme_project()` here is the full version of the simple `theme_project()` from the ggplot chapter: same name and `base_size` argument, plus a font, furniture colours and an `axis_type` argument. ## Audience must be determined first Identify the audience as one of `journal-lab-report`, `poster`, `talk`, or `public-engagement` before writing any plotting code. Styling, annotation density, and title framing all depend on the answer. If the audience is not specified, ask (see *Missing information*). If proceeding without an answer, default to `journal-lab-report` and record the assumption at the top of the script: ```r # Audience not specified; defaulting to journal-lab-report. # Re-run with explicit audience if poster, talk, or public-engagement intended. ``` Then state in one sentence each: the variables and their types (continuous, discrete, date/time), the scientific question, the chart type the variable structure calls for, whether raw data will be shown, and whether statistical annotations are required. ## Statistical annotations require a model object Do not annotate test statistics, p-values, or confidence intervals unless a fitted model object exists: fitted by code in this project that you have run or can read, or present in the user's live R session where your tool can see it. Fabricating values from descriptive data is a serious error. If there is no model, omit annotations and insert this placeholder for the legend: > LEGEND PLACEHOLDER. Model object required to supply the test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and adjustment method. Do not fabricate. ## Chart selection | Variable 1 | Variable 2 | Variable 3 | Default chart | |------------|------------|------------|---------------| | Continuous | — | — | Raincloud (`ggdist::stat_halfeye` + boxplot + jitter) | | Continuous | Continuous | — | Scatter plot | | Continuous | Continuous | Discrete | Scatter, colour and shape mapped to discrete | | Discrete | — | — | Bar chart of counts | | Discrete | Continuous | — | Raincloud per group; boxplot if many groups; bar only if one summary value per group | | Discrete | Discrete | — | Heatmap of counts | | Discrete | Discrete | Continuous | Heatmap of the continuous variable | | Date | Continuous | — | Line chart | | Date | Continuous | Discrete | Line chart, one line per group | If a chart not in this table is requested, select the closest matching entry, generate the code, and record both the request and the substitution in a comment at the top of the script (and in the pull request description, if there is one). ## Colour The colour-vision-deficiency check (`cvdPlot()`, below) is the final arbiter: a palette that fails it must be replaced, regardless of brand intent. **No brand specified (default).** Use `colorspace::scale_*` functions, matched to data structure. **Brand specified.** When the request names a brand colour (for example, "use a brand colour of darkblue"), call `set_brand("darkblue")` once after sourcing `theme-project.R`. `set_brand()` accepts any R colour name or hex string. The brand colour then seeds: - single-colour and highlight geoms, via `brand_base()`; - sequential continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_seq()`; - the **high** arm of diverging continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_div(midpoint = )`. The low arm is the brand's complementary hue, so the two arms always contrast, unless you name a second brand colour with `set_brand(, div_low = )`. **Categorical colour is never brand-seeded.** One seed colour cannot generate a coherent, CVD-safe set of distinct hues. For unordered groups, use `colorspace` "Dark 2"; `scale_*_brand_qual()` in `theme-project.R` is the same palette and takes no `base` or `n` argument. The brand colour can still mark one focal group, with the other groups in grey. | Data structure | Palette type | colorspace default | With a brand set | |----------------|--------------|--------------------|------------------| | Discrete, unordered groups | Qualitative | `Dark 2` | `Dark 2` (`scale_*_brand_qual()` is identical) | | Discrete, ordered groups | Sequential discrete | `Purples 3` | `Purples 3` (the brand scales are continuous only) | | Continuous, one-directional | Sequential | `Viridis` | `scale_*_brand_seq()` | | Continuous, midpoint-centred | Diverging | `Blue-Red` | `scale_*_brand_div()` | If a brand-seeded scale fails the CVD check, replace it with the colorspace default in the same row and record the fallback in a comment. Categorical groupings must use redundant encoding: shape for points, linetype for lines. Colour alone is not sufficient. ## Audience-specific styling | Element | Journal / lab report | Poster | Talk | Public engagement | |---------|---------------------|--------|------|-------------------| | Title above figure | No | Yes (explanatory) | Yes (explanatory) | Yes (explanatory) | | Figure legend below | Yes (four elements) | Optional, abbreviated | No | No | | Direct labelling | Sparingly | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Highlighting (grey out non-focal) | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Reference lines | Sparingly | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Statistical annotations | Precise p-values | Abbreviated | One key result | None | | Base font size | 12 pt floor | 16 to 20 pt | 14 to 18 pt | 14 to 18 pt | | Raw data shown | Always where n permits | Always | Always | Where it clarifies | `theme_project()` defaults to `base_size = 12`, the journal/lab-report floor. Raise it explicitly via `theme_project(base_size = ...)` for poster, talk, and public-engagement figures per this table. Descriptive titles state what the figure shows. Explanatory titles state what it means. Journal figures put descriptive framing in the legend, not the title. ## Showing raw data | n per group | Display | |-------------|---------| | Up to ~30 | Strip plot or raincloud, all points visible | | ~30 to ~300 | Raincloud with jittered points, alpha 0.3 to 0.5 | | ~300 to ~3000 | Beeswarm or 2D density | | > ~3000 | Hexbin or 2D contour | ## Statistical annotations workflow Pairwise contrasts come from `emmeans::emmeans()` and `emmeans::pairs()` with an explicit adjustment method (`tukey`, `holm`, or similar). Render brackets with `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()`, supplying a data frame of contrasts. Filter to significant contrasts before drawing. Format p-values with `scales::label_pvalue()` so very small values appear as `<0.001` rather than `0.000`. A worked example is in `emmeans-bridge.R`. ## Error bars Three options, not interchangeable: - **Standard deviation:** spread of individual observations. Use when describing population variability. - **Standard error of the mean:** precision of the sample mean. Shrinks with sample size. - **95% confidence interval:** the recommended default. Prefer model-based intervals via `emmeans` where a model exists, otherwise from `stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal)`. The choice must appear in the y axis label. ## Multiple panels and shared legends When composing panels with `patchwork` and `plot_layout(guides = "collect")`, collection merges only guides that are identical in aesthetic, scale, breaks, and title (`name`). It deduplicates by guide specification, not by visual appearance, and it never removes a guide it judges different. Two failures follow: panels that encode the same variable through different aesthetics (`fill` in one, `colour` plus `shape` in another) or different palettes produce one legend each; and a panel encoding a genuinely different variable produces its own legend, which is correct. Resolve the layout from the plot specifications: - **Same variable, same palette, across all panels:** produce one shared legend. Designate the panel with the richest encoding (e.g. colour plus shape) as the legend-bearer, because that legend is a complete key for the simpler panels but not the reverse. Apply the identical scale call and an identical `name` in every panel, then suppress the guide on every non-bearing panel with `guides( = "none")`. Record the choice of bearer in a comment. - **Panels encode different variables:** do not force collection into one key. Keep the separate legends; merging them would mislabel a panel. A mismatched `name`, a differing aesthetic or scale, or a missing suppression line will silently leave more than one legend for the same variable. After composing, confirm exactly one legend appears per distinct variable. A worked skeleton is in `patchwork-template.R`. ## Saving Always save to `outputs/figures/` via `here::here()` in both PDF and PNG formats. Specify `width`, `height`, `units`, and `dpi` explicitly; do not rely on `ggsave()` defaults. Use `ragg::agg_png` as the device for PNG output with `bg = "white"`. PDF uses the default device. ## Accessibility check The agent cannot verify visual accessibility. Insert this line at the end of the script and flag it for the investigator to run and inspect: ```r colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1) ``` If the four-panel simulation shows groups becoming indistinguishable under deuteranopia, protanopia, or tritanopia, the palette or redundant encoding must be revised. For brand-seeded scales, a failed check requires falling back to the `colorspace` default named in the colour table; brand intent does not override accessibility. ## Pre-flight checklist (agent-verifiable items only) Before declaring the script complete, confirm: - Both axes labelled with name and unit, or just name for dimensionless variables. - Bar chart axes start at zero; other axes cropped to the data range. - Faceted panels share scale unless a comment justifies freeing it. - Composite figures collect to one legend per distinct variable; non-bearing panels suppress their guide with `guides(... = "none")` and all retained scales share an identical `name`. - Palette applied via `colorspace::scale_*` functions or the brand-seeded constructors in `theme-project.R`, never hand-written hex vectors as data scales. Single fixed colours for single-group or highlight geoms are permitted. - Categorical colour uses `Dark 2` (directly or via `scale_*_brand_qual()`), not a brand-seeded palette. - A brand-seeded scale that the colour-vision-deficiency check would fail is replaced by its `colorspace` default; the fallback is recorded in a comment. - Categorical grouping carries redundant encoding (shape or linetype). - Statistical annotations sourced from a fitted model object, never from descriptive data. - None of the forbidden chart types in *House rules*. - Default theme is `theme_project()`, `theme_minimal()`, or `theme_classic()`. Never `theme_grey()`. - `theme_project()` base font size matches the audience floor (12 pt journal; 14 to 20 pt otherwise). - File saved to `outputs/figures/` as both PDF and PNG with explicit dimensions. - `cvdPlot()` call inserted at the end of the script with a comment flagging it for the investigator. ## Supplementary files in this skill directory - `raincloud-template.R`: figure skeleton with palette, theme, and saving. - `emmeans-bridge.R`: worked emmeans-to-ggpubr annotation pattern. - `theme-project.R`: project theme plus brand-seeded HCL palette constructors. - `patchwork-template.R`: composite-figure skeleton with collected legend and guide suppression. ```` ::: ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/theme-project.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # ============================================================================== # Project theme and palette construction for ggplot2. # # Colour policy (authoritative; see pub-figures SKILL.md): # * No brand set -> use colorspace palettes directly. # * Brand set -> set_brand("darkblue") sets the base colour (used by # single-colour and highlight geoms) and reseeds the # sequential ramp and the diverging HIGH arm. The # low arm becomes the brand's complementary hue # unless set_brand() is given div_low. Sequential # and diverging are # generated via colorspace HCL generators # (CVD-robust, monotonic luminance). # * Categorical colour is NEVER brand-seeded: scale_*_brand_qual() delegate to # colorspace "Dark 2", which sizes itself to the data. # A single seed cannot make a coherent multi-hue set. # * Single-group / highlight geoms default to brand_base(), teal until reset. # # Manual hex palettes are NOT used as data scales. Only the base colour is used # directly, and only for single-colour or highlight geoms. # # theme_project() here is the full version of the simple theme_project() taught # in the ggplot chapter (Block 3: Themes and scales). Accepts any R colour name or hex string. .brand_state <- new.env(parent = emptyenv()) .brand_state$base <- "#09baba" # teal default .brand_state$div_low <- "#2c4977" # navy default for the diverging low arm #' Normalise a colour name or hex to a hex string #' @keywords internal .as_hex <- function(col) { rgb <- grDevices::col2rgb(col) # accepts R colour names and hex grDevices::rgb(rgb[1], rgb[2], rgb[3], maxColorValue = 255) } #' Set the project brand colour #' #' Sets the base colour used by single-colour and highlight geoms, the #' sequential ramp and the diverging high arm. Call once at the top of a #' script: `set_brand("darkblue")`. Accepts any R colour name or hex string. #' #' @param base Brand colour (name or hex). #' @param div_low Optional colour for the diverging low arm. If `NULL` (the #' default), the low arm uses the hue opposite the brand colour on the HCL #' colour wheel, so the two arms always contrast. #' @return Invisibly, the resolved brand state as a list. #' @export set_brand <- function(base, div_low = NULL) { .brand_state$base <- .as_hex(base) .brand_state$div_low <- if (is.null(div_low)) { .complement_of(.brand_state$base) } else { .as_hex(div_low) } invisible(as.list(.brand_state)) } #' Colour with the opposite HCL hue, for the diverging low arm #' @keywords internal .complement_of <- function(col) { hue <- (.hue_of(col) + 180) %% 360 colorspace::hex(colorspace::polarLUV(L = 40, C = 60, H = hue), fixup = TRUE) } #' Reset the brand to the teal/navy default #' @return Invisibly, the resolved brand state as a list. #' @export reset_brand <- function() { .brand_state$base <- "#09baba" .brand_state$div_low <- "#2c4977" invisible(as.list(.brand_state)) } #' Current brand base colour #' #' Returns the current brand base as a hex string. It is a function, not a value, #' so it reflects the most recent `set_brand()` call. Use as `brand_base()`. #' @return A hex colour string. #' @export brand_base <- function() .brand_state$base # ---- Internal: font registration --------------------------------------------- # Returns TRUE if `family` is available to showtext, FALSE otherwise, so the # theme can fall back to the device's default font rather than warn on every # text element. .register_project_font <- function(family = "Open Sans") { if (!requireNamespace("showtext", quietly = TRUE)) { return(FALSE) } showtext::showtext_auto(enable = TRUE) if (!(family %in% sysfonts::font_families())) { try(sysfonts::font_add_google(family, family), silent = TRUE) } family %in% sysfonts::font_families() } # ---- theme_project() --------------------------------------------------------- #' Project theme #' #' A composable ggplot2 theme controlling non-data aesthetics only. It sets no #' data-encoding colours; pair it with a scale constructor (see below). Furniture #' colours (title, axis labels, gridlines) are decorative and need not be #' CVD-safe; the strip background is deliberately neutral grey so it is not #' mistaken for a data signal when a fill palette is present. Furniture colours do #' not track the brand by design; rebrand them by editing the literals below. #' #' @param base_size Base font size in points. Default 12 (journal/lab-report #' floor; raise to 14-20 for poster, talk, or public-engagement). #' @param base_family Base font family. Default "Open Sans". #' @param base_line_size Base line size. Default 0.5. #' @param base_rect_size Base rectangle size. Default 0.5. #' @param axis_type "categorical" or "continuous"; controls gridlines. #' @return A ggplot2 theme object. #' @export theme_project <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "Open Sans", base_line_size = 0.5, base_rect_size = 0.5, axis_type = c("categorical", "continuous")) { axis_type <- match.arg(axis_type) if (!.register_project_font(base_family)) { base_family <- "" # device default font } title_col <- "#2c4977" # decorative furniture only label_col <- "#41566f" muted_col <- "#5d6b7d" base <- ggplot2::theme( line = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "#000000", linewidth = base_line_size), rect = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", colour = "#000000", linewidth = base_rect_size), text = ggplot2::element_text(family = base_family, colour = "#000000", size = base_size), plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, size = ggplot2::rel(1.4), margin = ggplot2::margin(8, 0, 6, 0), colour = title_col), plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0, size = ggplot2::rel(1.1), margin = ggplot2::margin(2, 0, 0, 0), colour = label_col), plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 1, size = ggplot2::rel(0.8), margin = ggplot2::margin(6, 0, 0, 0), colour = muted_col), axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = muted_col, size = ggplot2::rel(0.9)), axis.title.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = label_col, margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 4, 0, 0)), axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(colour = muted_col, size = ggplot2::rel(0.9)), axis.title.x = ggplot2::element_text(colour = label_col, margin = ggplot2::margin(4, 0, 0, 0)), panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA), strip.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#e9e9e9", colour = NA), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#2c4977", size = ggplot2::rel(1.0)), panel.border = ggplot2::element_blank(), axis.line = ggplot2::element_line(linewidth = base_line_size, colour = "black"), legend.position = "right" ) grid_col <- "#dedddd" if (axis_type == "continuous") { grid_theme <- ggplot2::theme( panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col), panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col) ) } else { grid_theme <- ggplot2::theme( panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col), panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank() ) } base + grid_theme } # ---- Brand-seeded palette constructors --------------------------------------- # These wrap colorspace HCL generators, seeded on the current brand colour, so # the ramp is perceptually based with monotonic luminance. With no set_brand() # call the seed is teal; callers may also pass `base`/`low`/`high` explicitly, # which always overrides the brand state. If no brand is intended at all, use # colorspace::scale_*_{qualitative,sequential,diverging} directly. #' Hue (HCL) of a colour, for seeding colorspace generators #' @keywords internal .hue_of <- function(col) { hcl <- colorspace::coords(as(colorspace::hex2RGB(.as_hex(col)), "polarLUV")) unname(hcl[, "H"]) } #' Brand-seeded sequential scale (colour) #' #' Single-hue sequential ramp seeded on `base`, generated in HCL so luminance is #' monotonic. Light-to-dark by default. #' #' @param base Seed colour. Defaults to the current `brand_base()`. #' @param n Number of interpolation stops. Default 7. #' @param ... Passed to `ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn()`. #' @return A ggplot2 scale. #' @export scale_colour_brand_seq <- function(base = brand_base(), n = 7, ...) { cols <- colorspace::sequential_hcl( n = n, h = .hue_of(base), c = c(70, 10), l = c(25, 95), power = 1.2, rev = TRUE ) ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn(colours = cols, ...) } #' @rdname scale_colour_brand_seq #' @export scale_fill_brand_seq <- function(base = brand_base(), n = 7, ...) { cols <- colorspace::sequential_hcl( n = n, h = .hue_of(base), c = c(70, 10), l = c(25, 95), power = 1.2, rev = TRUE ) ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(colours = cols, ...) } #' Brand-seeded diverging scale (colour) #' #' Two-hue diverging ramp seeded on `low` and `high`, generated in HCL with a #' balanced neutral midpoint. Supply `midpoint` to centre on a meaningful value. #' #' @param low Seed colour for the low arm. Defaults to navy or, after #' `set_brand()`, to the brand's complementary hue (or its `div_low`). #' @param high Seed colour for the high arm. Defaults to the current `brand_base()`. #' @param midpoint Data value mapped to the neutral midpoint. Default 0. #' @param n Number of interpolation stops (odd recommended). Default 11. #' @param ... Passed to `ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn()`. #' @return A ggplot2 scale. #' @export scale_colour_brand_div <- function(low = .brand_state$div_low, high = brand_base(), midpoint = 0, n = 11, ...) { cols <- colorspace::diverging_hcl( n = n, h = c(.hue_of(low), .hue_of(high)), c = 80, l = c(35, 95), power = 1.0 ) ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn( colours = cols, rescaler = ~ scales::rescale_mid(.x, mid = midpoint), ... ) } #' @rdname scale_colour_brand_div #' @export scale_fill_brand_div <- function(low = .brand_state$div_low, high = brand_base(), midpoint = 0, n = 11, ...) { cols <- colorspace::diverging_hcl( n = n, h = c(.hue_of(low), .hue_of(high)), c = 80, l = c(35, 95), power = 1.0 ) ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn( colours = cols, rescaler = ~ scales::rescale_mid(.x, mid = midpoint), ... ) } #' Qualitative scale (colour) for categorical groups #' #' Categorical palettes are NOT brand-seeded. A single brand colour cannot #' generate a coherent, CVD-safe multi-hue set: spreading hues from one anchor #' discards the seed's own chroma and luminance and walks through arbitrary #' intermediate hues. This constructor therefore delegates to `colorspace`'s #' `Dark 2` qualitative palette, which is built for mutual distinctness and is #' CVD-tested, and which sizes itself to the number of groups (so it cannot raise #' "Insufficient values in manual scale"). Reserve the brand colour for the #' sequential ramp, the diverging high arm, and single-colour or highlight geoms, #' where one seed genuinely works. Always pair with a redundant aesthetic (shape #' or linetype). #' #' @param ... Passed to `colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative()`. #' @return A ggplot2 scale. #' @export scale_colour_brand_qual <- function(...) { colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", ...) } #' @rdname scale_colour_brand_qual #' @param ... Passed to `colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative()`. #' @export scale_fill_brand_qual <- function(...) { colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", ...) } # ---- Example usage ----------------------------------------------------------- # Set a brand once, then everything downstream follows: # set_brand("darkblue") # ... + scale_fill_brand_seq() # darkblue-seeded sequential # ... + geom_point(colour = brand_base())# darkblue single-colour geom # ... + scale_fill_brand_div(midpoint = 0) # complementary low arm, darkblue high # # No brand (default path): colorspace directly. # ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = g, shape = g)) + geom_point() + # colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") + # theme_project(axis_type = "continuous") # # Per-call override (ignores brand state): # ... + scale_fill_brand_seq(base = "#2c4977") # # Accessibility check is mandatory; a brand-seeded palette that fails it falls # back to its colorspace default (Viridis for sequential, Blue-Red for diverging): # colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1) ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/raincloud-template.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # raincloud-template.R # Figure skeleton: raincloud for Discrete x Continuous, with palette, theme # and saving. # Audience not specified; defaulting to journal-lab-report. # Re-run with explicit audience if poster, talk, or public-engagement intended. # # Colour policy (see pub-figures SKILL.md): # * Groups are categorical, so colour comes from colorspace qualitative # "Dark 2" whether or not a brand is set. Categorical colour is never # brand-seeded; scale_*_brand_qual() in theme-project.R is the same palette. # * If a brand is set with set_brand(), use brand_base() only for # single-colour or highlight geoms. library(ggplot2) library(ggdist) library(colorspace) library(here) library(scales) # The skill's single copy lives in .agents/skills/. If you copied the folder # into .claude/skills/ instead of linking it, change this path to match. source(here::here(".agents", "skills", "pub-figures", "theme-project.R")) # data |> expects: group (factor), value (numeric) fig1 <- data |> ggplot(aes(x = group, y = value, colour = group, shape = group)) + ggdist::stat_halfeye( aes(fill = group), adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.5 ) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) + geom_point( position = position_jitter(width = 0.05, seed = 1), alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5 ) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") + colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") + scale_shape_discrete() + # redundant encoding alongside colour labs(x = NULL, y = "Value (unit)") + theme_project() # Save as PDF and PNG with explicit dimensions ---- fig_dir <- here::here("outputs", "figures") dir.create(fig_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) ggsave( file.path(fig_dir, "fig1.pdf"), fig1, width = 160, height = 110, units = "mm" ) ggsave( file.path(fig_dir, "fig1.png"), fig1, width = 160, height = 110, units = "mm", dpi = 300, device = ragg::agg_png, bg = "white" ) # Accessibility check; investigator to run and inspect. colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1) ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/emmeans-bridge.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # emmeans-bridge.R # Worked emmeans-to-ggpubr annotation pattern. # Requires a fitted model object: fitted by code in this project that you have # run or can read, or present in the user's live R session where your tool can # see it. Never fabricate test statistics from descriptive data. library(emmeans) library(ggpubr) library(dplyr) library(tibble) library(tidyr) library(stringr) library(ggplot2) library(scales) # model <- lm(value ~ group, data = data) # supplied upstream # fig1 <- ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) + geom_boxplot() # supplied upstream # # ADAPT: `fig1` is your existing ggplot. `panel_yrange()` reads layer 1 by # default, which must be the geom whose data the brackets sit above (e.g. the # boxplot). If layer 1 is a reference line or similar, pass the correct index, # e.g. panel_yrange(fig1, layer = 2L). emm <- emmeans::emmeans(model, specs = "group") # lowest and highest y values drawn by one layer ---- panel_yrange <- function(p, layer = 1L) { d <- ggplot2::ggplot_build(p)$data[[layer]] # positional y columns ggplot may compute cols <- intersect( c("ymin_final", "ymin", "lower", "ymax_final", "ymax", "upper", "y"), names(d) ) if (length(cols) == 0L) { stop("No y-position column found in layer ", layer, ".") } range(unlist(d[cols]), na.rm = TRUE) } y_range <- panel_yrange(fig1) # step between brackets as a fraction of the data range, so positions work for # negative values and for data far from zero y_step <- 0.07 * diff(y_range) contrasts_df <- pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey") |> as_tibble() |> separate_wider_delim( contrast, delim = " - ", names = c("group1", "group2") ) |> # emmeans wraps level names containing spaces or operators in parentheses dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across( c(group1, group2), \(x) stringr::str_remove_all(x, "^\\(|\\)$") )) |> dplyr::filter(p.value < 0.05) |> dplyr::mutate( p.label = scales::label_pvalue()(p.value), y.position = y_range[2] + y_step * dplyr::row_number() ) # headroom so the top bracket isn't clipped: highest position + one more step y_top <- y_range[2] + y_step * (nrow(contrasts_df) + 1) fig1 + stat_pvalue_manual( contrasts_df, label = "p.label", tip.length = 0.01 ) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(NA, y_top)) ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `pub-figures/patchwork-template.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Composite figure: panels sharing ONE collected legend. # # Precondition: every panel maps the SAME grouping variable to the SAME palette. # If a panel encodes a different variable, do not use this pattern for it; give it # its own scale and accept a separate legend (forcing one key would mislabel it). # # Colour policy (see pub-figures SKILL.md): # * The shared grouping variable is categorical, so every panel uses # colorspace qualitative "Dark 2", with or without a brand. Categorical # colour is never brand-seeded. Keep an identical `name` across panels so # the legend collects to one. # # Legend-bearer: chosen here by richness of encoding. If unclear, use the panel # with the most aesthetics mapped to the group and record the choice. # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- library(ggplot2) library(patchwork) # Legend-bearing panel: richest encoding (colour + shape), legend retained. # Redundant encoding (shape) is required by the skill, and conveniently makes this # panel a complete key for the simpler ones. p_keep <- data |> ggplot(aes(x = x1, y = y1, colour = group_var, shape = group_var)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") + scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15), name = "Group") + labs(x = "X1", y = "Y1") # Other panels: identical palette and identical name, guide suppressed. # Suppression is what collection cannot do for you. Repeat per additional panel. p_other <- data |> ggplot(aes(x = x2, y = y2, colour = group_var)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") + labs(x = "X2", y = "Y2") + guides(colour = "none") # Letters refer to plots in the order added (A = p_keep, B = p_other). layout <- " AB " fig1 <- p_keep + p_other + patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") & theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)) fig1 ``` ::: ::: ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
canary A fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.
front matter The block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill's name and description, or a Quarto document's options.
instruction file A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.
skill A folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.
symbolic link A file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler.
